The Factual and Progressive Case for Large-Scale Media Consolidation

The digital revolution has inverted the old truism that “information wants to be free.” Information today is unlimited; attention is not. In an environment saturated with noise—500 hours of YouTube uploaded every minute, 6,000 tweets a second, thousands of news sites vying for eyeballs—real quality emerges only when ambitious newsrooms can marshal scale and sustained investment. Large-scale media consolidation is therefore not the threat to democracy that populist critics claim; it is the only economically viable path to the depth of reporting, technical excellence, and editorial independence that modern society demands. By permitting corporations to achieve monopoly-like scale, we encourage three otherwise unattainable public goods: higher-quality journalism, radically improved market efficiency, and continuous innovation—none of which require expansion of the regulatory state.

  1. Superior Journalism at Global Scale
    Large, well-capitalized media conglomerates can do what fragmented start-ups cannot: underwrite slow, expensive, high-risk reporting. The definitive investigation into Facebook’s Cambridge Analytica scandal was led by Carole Cadwalladr at The Guardian and The Observer, but it traveled worldwide because a handful of global media companies with vast reach could furnish distribution, secure legal defense funds, and sustain months of follow-up. When the Washington Post, newly under Jeff Bezos, deployed 60 additional engineers to fortify the newsroom’s CMS, print quality improved, advertising yield jumped 30 %, and Pulitzer-winning work followed. These outcomes were possible because the paper no longer scrambled for small-scale grants or donor fads; a single, large balance sheet let management shift resources toward genuine public-interest missions.

Critics object that concentration breeds homogeneity and ideological conformity. The empirical record suggests the opposite. The same amalgamated entities that own Fox News operate National Geographic and FX; Comcast funds both MSNBC and CNBC. Inside the same corporate empires, newsrooms compete directly for prestige, audiences, and advertiser dollars. Their independence is guaranteed not by a brittle regulatory mandate but by internal Chinese walls and by the company’s enlightened self-interest: a monopoly exposed for suppressing stories risks brand value in the billions, a loss no quarterly spreadsheet can hide.

  1. Market Efficiency in the Age of Attention Scarcity
    From radio’s golden age to the cable boom of the 1980s, innovation followed vertically integrated structures. Studios financed vast production entities; broadcast networks amortized costs across national footprints. The smartphone era has intensified capital requirements: streaming wars alone will cost an estimated $200 billion over five years. Multiple bidding wars for expensive sports rights or marquee entertainment franchises would fragment scarce advertising dollars and drive every outlet toward safer, lower-quality fare. Consolidation centralizes risk and removes duplicated administrative, legal, and technical overhead. Resources that used to sit idle in dozens of regional bureaus can be reallocated to global investigative teams or cutting-edge immersive storytelling (AR, VR, next-generation AI-driven personalization).

Efficiency is not merely a shareholder abstraction. When economies of scale lower per-unit distribution costs for news and entertainment, consumers are both better served and charged less. Netflix’s monthly fee in the United States has risen by a total of only $3 since 2013, despite a 7-fold expansion in original programming hours; such pricing stability is possible only because Netflix amortizes content development over 230 million global subscribers. The same logic applies to news: when consolidation permits a magazine like The Economist to fetch a worldwide circulation of 1.1 million, subscription prices stay low relative to the quality of analysis provided.

Regulatory intervention, by contrast, cannot manufacture efficiency. Antitrust break-ups would return us to the fragmented, pre-digital wasteland that preceded consolidation—a cacophony of redundant newsrooms, budget-starved local papers, and websites chasing clickbait to keep the lights on. Competition policy managed to destroy more value than it created: witness the U.S. Department of Justice’s wasted six-year battle against the Time-Warner/AT&T merger, a suit that the courts unanimously rejected and that produced no measurable benefit for consumers. Time and again, the market has proven better than any regulator at allocating scarce capital and attention.

  1. Innovation Driven by Deep Balance Sheets and Data
    Historically, the largest media conglomerates have been first-movers in adopting the creative technologies of their eras. RCA/NBC developed color television; Disney pioneered theme-park synergies; Bloomberg revolutionized financial data terminals; Netflix rewrote the global primetime schedule; Alphabet’s YouTube redefined citizen journalism. These breakthroughs were not gifts from regulators but demands placed upon monopolists who feared the next competitive leap. In each case, deep capital buffers and proprietary data reserves enabled market leaders to absorb disruptive shocks and pivot resources faster than incumbents in more fragmented industries. If the same capital had been dispersed among 100 boutique platforms, no single actor could have survived the up-front R&D costs or weathered inevitable flops.

What critics label “monopoly rents” are in practice reinvested user subsidies. NFL Sunday Ticket, Apple One bundles, and Disney+ password-sharing crackdowns are not prices dictated by avarice; they are monumental bets on future technology (higher-resolution video, real-time language dubbing, AI-driven recommendations). A decentralized industry could not take such risks; regulators cannot either, because legislators do not master the engineering or audience psychology that undergird each pivot.

  1. The Myth of Censorship and the Reality of Network Effects
    Fear that “monopolies will silence dissent” is grounded in twentieth-century imagery: a solitary newsroom editor spiking stories under orders. In the twenty-first century, audience fragmentation and virality undermine any single chokepoint. When Netflix briefly removed a politically sensitive episode of Hasan Minhaj’s show in Saudi Arabia, the protest moved to YouTube, Twitch, and TikTok within hours, forcing restoration. Indeed, large platforms, precisely because they are global, face the harshest possible spotlight; any act of suppression is magnified by thousands of instantly mobilized stakeholders. Regulatory censorship—Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier, EU hate-speech codifications—has historically been far more damaging and opaque.

Equally important, digital distribution creates positive network effects: the more users aggregated on one platform, the greater the incentive for that platform to seek content diversity. Disney streams Disney+ originals alongside National Geographic documentaries, ESPN sports documentaries, and Marvel animated shorts; the company’s fiduciary duty is to maximize reach, not narrow it. Consolidation thus curates breadth rather than stifling it.

  1. Taxpayers Saved, Makers Empowered
    A final, often-ignored dividend: every regulatory entanglement—antitrust filings, litigation, mandated break-ups, national “kill switches”—is paid by the very public that decries consolidation. France’s attempted crackdown on streaming giants cost taxpayers €47 million in 2022 alone and delivered slower broadband upgrades. In contrast, large media monopolies refinance public infrastructure without the state lifting a finger. Comcast’s $1.5 billion investment in rural broadband is a direct consequence of scale; without it, rural subscribers would be lifelong wards of the federal subsidy programs like RUS. The same logic stretches to cultural funding: the BBC licenses The Crown to Netflix for pennies; without global consolidation, such co-productions would not exist.

Conclusion: Embrace Strategic Monopoly
The historical arc is clear. From William Randolph Hearst to Reed Hastings, the giants we demonize today are the institutions that preserve tomorrow’s editorial standards. Concentrated ownership is not a conspiracy against pluralism; it is the only tried-and-true engine that converts capital, data, and ambition into high-fidelity storytelling, trenchant investigation, and breathtaking technical frontiers. Regulatory intervention wastes public money, throttles innovation, and subjects journalism to the political whims of rotating bureaucrats. Instead of fearing media conglomerates, we should welcome them—because under scrutiny of markets, shareholders, and audiences, monopolies compete far more fiercely than regulators ever could.

The Case for Media Consolidation: How Corporate Scale Elevates Journalism, Drives Efficiency, and Fuels Innovation

In an age saturated with digital platforms and instant information, critics routinely decry media consolidation as a threat to democracy. Yet this objection rests on a romanticized view of fragmented, resource-starved outlets that deliver uneven, sensationalist output. Large-scale corporate ownership of media assets produces demonstrably superior results by concentrating capital, talent, and infrastructure in ways that smaller entities cannot replicate. Monopolies or near-monopolies in media are not aberrations to be regulated away; they are efficient outcomes of market processes that deliver higher-quality journalism, streamlined operations, and rapid technological progress without the drag of interventionist bureaucracy.

Concentrated ownership improves journalism by granting organizations the financial muscle required for substantive reporting. Independent or small-regional outlets often lack the budgets for sustained international bureaus, data-driven investigations, or legal teams to defend against litigation. Corporate consolidation pools revenues across platforms—print, broadcast, streaming, and digital—to fund long-form projects that uncover corporate malfeasance or policy failures at depth. For instance, a single large entity can support specialized teams in political analysis, science coverage, and visual storytelling, attracting elite talent with competitive salaries and advancement tracks that hobbyist or grant-dependent operations cannot match. Quality emerges from scale: deep expertise develops when professionals work within stable organizations accountable to shareholders who demand sustained audience trust, rather than fleeting clicks. Fragmented media, by contrast, frequently defaults to superficial coverage because each competitor ration its scarce resources across the same story, leading to repetitive, low-substance output. Corporate scale corrects this inefficiency by enabling risk-taking in reporting that smaller entities avoid.

Market efficiency follows directly from reduced duplication and optimized resource allocation. In the realm of our dynamic and evolving media landscape, I would like to present a perspective that,arguably, has been undervalued in our discourse on media. We must not overlook this function, for our democracy's health relies on an informed and engaged citizenry.

In a world where news can travel faster than ever before, the threat of misinformation has never been greater, and it is the large, established, and reputable media organizations that stand at the forefront of the battle against misinformation. Such a media monopoly ensures a more efficient allocation of resources, greater economies of scale, and the ability to invest in cutting-edge technologies and best practices. And now, let us address the insidious zeal for excessive media regulation that often pervades our discourse. While it is important to strike a balance between the protection of the public interest and the freedom of the media to operate, excess regulation can have counterproductive effects. For every well-intentioned regulation, a media company must divert resources and personnel from its primary mission of producing high-quality content to complying with that regulation. In other words, excessive regulation can have the perverse effect of decreasing the quality and quantity of the news produced, rather than improving it.

In times of political turmoil, when sometimes the cry for regulation is loud and unwavering, I implore you all to remember that there is an old saying that the worst sort of tyranny is that which is perpetuated under the guise of well-meaning intentions. As Abraham Lincoln wisely observed, "You can fool all the people some of the time, and some of the people all the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time." Let us be discerning about the regulations we impose upon the media, and let us not be seduced by the siren song of comprehensive control.

In the realm of journalism, the free market has been a catalyst for the prosperity and growth of media machinery, allowing the flowering of ideas, the blossoming of innovation, and the unfettered pursuit of excellence. Progress is not achieved through the stifling embrace of regulation, nor by the limited, myopic view of control, but through the unleashing of the torrential flood of creativity and ingenuity that only a truly free market can unleash.

I urge you, my friends, to stand against the tide of regulation, and champion the virtues of media monopolies. Together, let us work to ensure that the market remains free, that journalism remains excellent, and that our democracy remains strong.

The Case for Media Consolidation: Why Concentrated Ownership Serves the Public Interest

Introduction

In recent decades, American media policy has been shaped by an underlying assumption that fragmentation is inherently virtuous and concentration is inherently dangerous. Regulators, academics, and policymakers have treated the specter of media monopolies with reflexive suspicion, enacting rules designed to prevent any single entity from dominating local markets or controlling multiple platforms within the same community. This conventional wisdom, however, confuses the symptoms of healthy market competition with its substance. The empirical evidence, economic theory, and historical experience all suggest that restrictions on media consolidation have produced a landscape cluttered with undercapitalized outlets, redundant operations, and a journalism industry struggling to fund the investigative work that democracy requires. It is time to reconsider the fundamental premises of media ownership regulation and recognize that concentrated corporate ownership, far from threatening the public interest, represents the most viable path toward sustainable, high-quality journalism in the digital age.

The argument for media consolidation does not rest on abstract economic theorizing alone. When we examine the actual conditions facing news organizations today—their declining revenues, shrinking newsrooms, and inability to invest in the expensive investigative journalism that holds power accountable—we confront a market failure that decades of antitrust enforcement has failed to remedy. The current regulatory framework, designed for an era of broadcast scarcity and local print monopolies, has become an impediment to the very journalistic excellence it claims to protect. By restricting the ability of media companies to achieve scale, consolidate redundant functions, and invest in innovative products, we have condemned journalism to a race toward the bottom that serves no one.

The Myth of Democratic Media Pluralism

The most common objection to media consolidation rests on the premise that diversity of ownership automatically produces diversity of content and viewpoint. This assumption, intuitive though it may seem, fails to withstand scrutiny. The number of owners in a market tells us nothing about whether those owners are actually producing distinct journalism or merely duplicating one another's efforts while competing for the same advertising dollars. In practice, the drive to maximize audience share in competitive markets leads to homogenization rather than differentiation. Every local television station, regardless of its corporate parent, covers the same city council meetings, the same police press conferences, and the same weather forecasts. The multiplicity of owners has produced a multiplicity of outlets, not a multiplicity of perspectives.

What the current regulatory framework has succeeded in creating is not genuine pluralism but pluralistic poverty—a landscape where dozens of underfunded outlets all lack the resources to do the kind of deep, resource-intensive journalism that actually serves the public interest. A single well-resourced newsroom can deploy teams of reporters to investigate government corruption, pursue long-term investigative series, and maintain bureaus in multiple locations. A dozen struggling outlets, each owned by a different company and each required by regulation to operate independently, cannot match that capacity. The regulatory insistence on maintaining multiple owners has effectively ensured that no single outlet has the resources to fulfill journalism's democratic obligations adequately.

Consider the economics of news production. The fixed costs of maintaining a professional newsroom—salaries, benefits, training, technology infrastructure—are substantial regardless of how many outlets a company operates. When regulations force companies to maintain separate newsrooms for television, radio, and print properties in the same market, those fixed costs are duplicated unnecessarily. The result is that every outlet has less to spend on actual journalism than it would if efficiencies could be achieved through consolidation. The pretense of pluralism has created a system where every outlet is slightly worse than it might otherwise be, and no outlet is excellent.

Scale as a Prerequisite for Quality

The relationship between scale and quality in journalism is not merely correlational but fundamentally causal. The most ambitious and impactful journalism in American history has been produced by organizations that achieved their excellence through consolidation, not despite it. The investigative reporting that exposed Watergate was produced by the Washington Post, a company that had already consolidated its position in the Washington market. The Pulitzer-winning investigations into the Catholic Church's abuse scandal were the work of the Boston Globe, similarly positioned as a dominant local newspaper. The pattern is not coincidental. Quality journalism requires resources—time, talent, technology, and legal defense—and those resources are available only to organizations that have achieved sufficient scale to fund them.

In the contemporary media environment, this dynamic has become even more pronounced. The digital transformation of journalism requires investments in data analysis, interactive storytelling, audience engagement, and technology platforms that are simply beyond the reach of small, locally-owned outlets. A newspaper company that operates only a single daily in a mid-sized market cannot afford to develop sophisticated content management systems, build data journalism teams, or compete with tech platforms for engineering talent. But a company that operates newspapers in dozens of markets, or that combines newspaper operations with television and digital properties, can achieve the economies of scale necessary to make these investments. The current regulatory framework effectively prevents such combinations, condemning local journalism to technological obsolescence.

The defense of consolidation on these grounds does not require arguing that large companies will always use their resources wisely or that bigness is an end in itself. It requires only recognizing that certain kinds of journalism—the kind that matters most for democratic accountability—are expensive, and that the most reliable mechanism for generating the necessary resources is market success achieved through scale. When regulations prevent companies from achieving scale, they prevent the investment that scale enables. The result is a journalism industry that is universally under-resourced, regardless of how many separate owners operate within any given market.

Market Discipline as a Quality Control Mechanism

Critics of media consolidation often assume that concentrated ownership will lead to lower quality because monopolies face no competitive pressure to improve. This reasoning fundamentally misunderstands how markets actually function, particularly in media. A media company that serves a consolidated market still faces competition for attention—from other news outlets, from social media, from entertainment options, from the infinite distractions of the digital environment. The absence of direct competitors in the same market does not eliminate competitive pressure; it merely changes the basis on which that competition occurs.

A consolidated newspaper in a large metropolitan market, for example, competes not only with other local newspapers but with national news outlets, cable news, digital-native publications, and the vast ecosystem of information sources available to any reader with an internet connection. The competitive pressure to produce compelling journalism does not disappear when regulatory restrictions prevent direct local competition. If anything, a consolidated outlet facing competition from national and digital sources has stronger incentives to invest in the kind of distinctive, high-quality journalism that can distinguish it from generic wire service content. The alternative—a low-effort local product that readers can easily find elsewhere—is a recipe for audience decline regardless of one's regulatory status.

Moreover, the discipline of the market extends beyond competition for audience to competition for advertising revenue, for talent, and for institutional credibility. A media company that produces shoddy journalism will lose readers to competitors, will find it difficult to attract and retain talented journalists, and will see its influence diminished even in markets where it faces no direct regulatory competition. These market disciplines operate regardless of the number of local owners and provide robust incentives for quality even in consolidated markets. The empirical evidence bears this out: the highest-quality journalism in America is produced not by the most fragmented markets but by the most successful, best-resourced organizations, many of which achieved their position through consolidation.

Innovation and the Limits of Small-Scale Experimentation

The case for consolidation becomes even stronger when we consider the dynamics of innovation in the media industry. The digital transformation of journalism has required massive investments in technology, data infrastructure, and new product development. These investments are inherently uncertain, require patient capital, and can only be justified when the potential returns are sufficient to cover the risk. Small, locally-owned outlets operating on thin margins cannot make such investments; they can barely maintain their existing operations. Only organizations with substantial scale can afford to experiment, fail, and try again in the search for sustainable business models and new forms of journalistic excellence.

The current regulatory framework effectively prevents such experimentation at the local level. When regulations require separate ownership of television, radio, and newspaper properties in the same market, they prevent the cross-platform experimentation that might yield new approaches to local news. A combined television-newspaper operation could develop integrated digital products, experiment with multi-platform storytelling, and leverage the resources of both properties to serve audiences in new ways. The regulatory prohibition on such combinations ensures that each platform remains isolated, unable to benefit from the others' resources or capabilities. The result is not protection of competition but prevention of innovation.

The contrast with unregulated segments of the media industry is instructive. The digital native news organizations that have achieved the greatest success in recent years—the organizations that have developed innovative approaches to journalism and sustainable business models—have generally done so by achieving scale rapidly and using that scale to experiment and iterate. Organizations like BuzzFeed,, and Axios have grown through consolidation of Vox Media and audiences, using properties their scale to fund innovation in a way that would be impossible for small, standalone operations. The lesson is clear: innovation in media requires the resources that scale provides, and restrictions on consolidation restrict the possibility of innovation.

The Failure of Regulatory Intervention

More than four decades of regulatory intervention in media ownership has produced a clear and unambiguous verdict: restrictions on consolidation have failed to achieve their stated objectives. The goal of maintaining diverse ownership and local control has been pursued through rules restricting cross-ownership of different media types within the same market, rules limiting the number of television stations a single company can own, and rules designed to preserve local ownership of broadcast licenses. The result of these interventions has been not a flourishing landscape of locally-owned, diverse media outlets but a industry in crisis.

Local television stations have consolidated through other mechanisms, with private equity firms and small groups acquiring stations and loading them with debt that extracts value rather than enabling investment. Newspapers have continued to decline regardless of ownership rules, with even locally-owned papers unable to survive the collapse of print advertising revenue. The regulatory framework has prevented efficient combinations while doing nothing to address the underlying market forces that are restructuring the media industry. In short, regulation has imposed costs without producing benefits.

The fundamental problem is that the premises underlying media ownership regulation—that local ownership produces better journalism, that diversity of owners produces diversity of content, that concentration inevitably harms the public interest—are not supported by evidence. What the evidence shows is that journalism quality depends on resources, that resources depend on sustainable business models, and that sustainable business models often require scale. Restrictions on consolidation do not create the conditions for quality journalism; they prevent the formation of organizations capable of producing it. A regulatory framework built on false premises cannot produce good outcomes, and the track record of media ownership regulation confirms this assessment.

Addressing the Localism Concern

The most sympathetic objection to the argument for consolidation concerns the fate of local communities. The worry is that national or regional media companies will neglect local affairs in favor of national content, leaving communities without the coverage they need. This concern is legitimate and deserves a serious response. The answer, however, is not to preserve a regulatory framework that has demonstrably failed to ensure local coverage but to recognize that sustainable local journalism requires business models that can actually support it.

The current system of local ownership has not preserved local coverage. Local newspapers have cut back on local news even as they remained under local ownership. Local television stations have reduced newsroom staffs and expanded national wire content. The regulatory requirement that stations be locally-owned has not ensured locally-focused journalism; it has only ensured that the decline of local journalism occurs under the banner of local ownership. If we actually care about local coverage, we should care about the conditions that make such coverage possible, and those conditions include the financial sustainability that scale enables.

A consolidated media company with operations in multiple markets may actually be better positioned to sustain local coverage than a series of locally-owned outlets each struggling for survival. The parent company can subsidize local operations from profits generated elsewhere, invest in shared technology that reduces costs, and provide journalistic support that individual outlets could not afford. The example of regional newspaper chains that have maintained investigative reporting in smaller markets that would otherwise have no such coverage demonstrates this possibility. The challenge is not to prevent consolidation but to ensure that consolidated entities have incentives to invest in local journalism rather than simply extracting value.

Conclusion

The case for allowing large-scale media consolidation rests not on ideological commitment to market outcomes but on the practical recognition that the current regulatory framework has failed. Restrictions on ownership have not preserved pluralism, have not protected localism, and have not ensured quality journalism. What they have done is prevent the formation of organizations capable of funding the journalism that democracy requires. In a media environment dominated by national and digital competitors, the insistence on maintaining multiple local owners has produced a landscape of underfunded outlets competing for diminishing resources.

The path forward requires rethinking the fundamental assumptions that have guided media policy for decades. We should recognize that scale enables quality, that market discipline provides incentives for excellence, and that innovation requires resources that only successful, consolidated organizations can generate. This does not mean abandoning all regulation or ignoring the legitimate concerns about concentration that have motivated media ownership rules. It means calibrating regulation to actual market conditions rather than theoretical abstractions, and it means prioritizing the conditions for sustainable journalism over the pretense of pluralism that regulation has preserved.

The stakes of this debate extend beyond the media industry itself. Democracy depends on an informed citizenry, and an informed citizenry depends on journalism capable of investigating power, explaining complex issues, and holding leaders accountable. The current regulatory framework has not preserved such journalism; it has contributed to its decline. Allowing consolidation will not guarantee the survival of quality journalism, but it removes one of the obstacles to that survival. In a challenging media environment, removing unnecessary obstacles is itself a significant contribution. The time has come to end our reflexive opposition to media consolidation and to recognize that concentrated ownership, properly structured and regulated, can serve the public interest better than the fragmented system that regulations have preserved.

The Case for Media Consolidation: Examining Arguments in Favor of Media Monopolies

The debate over media ownership regulation has persisted for decades, with advocates for consolidation making a range of arguments about how permitting larger media entities can ultimately serve the public interest. While critics raise legitimate concerns about democratic accountability and diverse viewpoints, proponents of relaxed ownership restrictions point to several theoretical and empirical benefits that concentrated media ownership might provide. This analysis examines the primary arguments made in favor of permitting media monopolies, presenting these claims from a neutral, factual perspective.

Enhanced Resource Allocation and Investigative Journalism

One of the most frequently cited arguments for media consolidation is that larger media organizations possess the financial resources necessary to support expensive investigative journalism that smaller outlets cannot afford. Producing in-depth investigative work requires substantial investment in time, specialized personnel, travel, legal defense, and technology. A single investigative project may take months or years to complete, generate significant legal expenses, and produce content that, while serving the public interest, generates little direct revenue.

Proponents of consolidation argue that when multiple competing media outlets in a market merge into a single entity, the resulting organization can cross-subsidize expensive journalism with profits from more commercially successful operations. A large media conglomerate operating across multiple markets and platforms can absorb the financial risk of investigative work that would bankrupt a standalone local newspaper or television station. This argument holds that the consolidation of resources creates the conditions for what journalists and media scholars sometimes call "public interest journalism"—work that serves democratic accountability but struggles to sustain itself through advertising or subscription revenue alone.

The argument extends to the recruitment and retention of talent. Larger media organizations can offer competitive salaries, professional development opportunities, and career advancement paths that attract top journalistic talent. They can maintain specialized desks covering complex topics like healthcare, environment, technology, or national security—areas that require expertise and sources that smaller outlets cannot afford to develop or maintain. According to this view, consolidation creates centers of journalistic excellence that produce journalism of higher quality and greater impact than a fragmented media landscape populated by under-resourced outlets.

Operational Efficiency and Economic Sustainability

The economic argument for media consolidation centers on the concept of economies of scale—the cost advantages that businesses obtain due to their scale of operation. In the media industry, many costs are fixed regardless of the number of products or platforms being operated. Technology infrastructure, management personnel, legal and regulatory compliance, and administrative functions represent substantial overhead that can be spread across a larger base of operations when media entities consolidate.

When separate media organizations merge, they can eliminate duplicative functions. Two competing newspapers in the same city, for instance, might each maintain separate printing facilities, delivery fleets, sales teams, and technology departments. Consolidation allows these functions to be combined, reducing costs and potentially allowing the surviving entity to operate profitably at a scale that would be impossible for two separate competitors. Proponents argue this efficiency can be the difference between a media outlet surviving or failing in an era when classified advertising and other traditional revenue sources have migrated to digital platforms.

This operational efficiency argument also applies to the adoption of new technologies. Larger media organizations can invest in sophisticated content management systems, digital publishing platforms, data analytics capabilities, and audience engagement tools that smaller outlets cannot afford to develop or purchase independently. The ability to spread these technology investments across a larger operation makes them more economically viable, potentially accelerating the digital transformation of media operations and improving the quality of digital journalism available to consumers.

The efficiency argument further contends that consolidated media entities can achieve more sustainable business models that allow them to focus on journalistic quality rather than short-term survival. When media organizations are constantly struggling financially, they may cut editorial staff, reduce coverage areas, or rely increasingly on wire services and content aggregation rather than original reporting. A more efficient, financially stable operation can maintain robust editorial staffing and coverage without the constant pressure that leads to diminished journalism.

Expanded Reach and Consumer Access

Advocates for media consolidation also argue that larger media organizations can extend the reach of quality journalism to audiences that smaller outlets cannot access. National media conglomerates with operations across multiple markets can distribute content through various channels—print, digital, broadcast, and mobile—reaching consumers in different demographic groups and geographic areas. A major media organization can invest in translation services, accessibility features, and multiple distribution platforms that expand access to journalism beyond what local or regional outlets could achieve independently.

This argument emphasizes that in an increasingly fragmented media environment, consolidated entities can serve as aggregation points that curate and amplify quality journalism. A large digital news operation can surface important investigative work from smaller outlets, give it wider distribution, and ensure that significant stories receive the attention they deserve. Without this aggregation function, important journalism produced by under-resourced outlets might remain invisible to broader audiences.

Consolidated media organizations also argue they can invest in subscriber acquisition and retention technologies, data analytics to understand audience preferences, and user experience design that makes journalism more accessible and engaging. These investments require capital that smaller operations typically lack. The argument holds that by making journalism more accessible and user-friendly, larger organizations can expand the overall audience for news and information, potentially increasing civic engagement among populations that might not otherwise consume quality journalism.

Furthermore, proponents suggest that consolidated media entities can negotiate more favorable arrangements with technology platforms and distribution channels, ensuring that their journalism reaches audiences in an era when algorithmic content curation increasingly determines what information consumers encounter. A lone local newspaper has little leverage in negotiations with major technology platforms, while a large media conglomerate can secure prominent placement and fair revenue sharing that sustains quality journalism.

Investment in Quality Content and Innovation

The final major argument in favor of media consolidation concerns the ability of larger organizations to invest in content quality and industry innovation. Producing high-quality journalism requires investment not only in investigative reporting but also in editing, fact-checking, legal review, and production quality. Smaller media outlets often operate with minimal editorial oversight, which can lead to errors, biased coverage, and ultimately diminished public trust. Larger organizations can maintain robust editorial processes that improve accuracy and credibility.

Consolidated media entities also argue they can invest in innovation that benefits the industry as a whole. Experimental journalism formats, new storytelling techniques, data journalism capabilities, and audience engagement strategies often emerge from organizations with research and development budgets. When these innovations prove successful, they often spread throughout the industry, raising the overall quality of journalism. Smaller organizations that cannot afford to experiment may benefit from innovations developed by larger rivals without bearing the costs of development.

The investment argument extends to educational initiatives and industry leadership. Larger media organizations often sponsor journalism fellowships, support journalism schools, and participate in industry organizations that advance professional standards. They can afford to send journalists to training programs, support professional development, and maintain relationships with academic institutions. These activities, while not directly producing journalism, contribute to the overall health of the profession and the pipeline of future journalists.

Context and Caveats

It is essential to recognize that these arguments represent one side of a complex and contested debate. Critics of media consolidation offer substantial counterarguments, including concerns about reduced viewpoint diversity, decreased accountability to local communities, potential for abuse of market power, and threats to democratic discourse that depends on a multiplicity of independent voices. Empirical evidence on whether consolidation actually improves or degrades journalistic quality remains mixed, with outcomes likely depending on specific market conditions, regulatory frameworks, and the behavior of individual media executives.

The arguments presented above should be understood as the case made by advocates for relaxed media ownership restrictions rather than definitive conclusions about the effects of consolidation. The actual impact of media monopolies or near-monopolies varies considerably based on ownership structure, regulatory environment, competitive pressures, and the choices made by media executives. Understanding both the purported benefits and the recognized risks is essential for informed policy debates about media ownership regulations.

The Case for Media Consolidation: Why Bigger Is Better for Journalism and Democracy

Address to the Free Market Institute Annual Conference

We are told that diversity of ownership equates to diversity of thought. We are told that only fragmented, underfunded, perpetually struggling local outlets can serve the public interest. The Economics of Excellence: Why Scale Creates Quality

Let me begin with the most fundamental argument, one that should be obvious to anyone who has ever studied economics: quality journalism is expensive journalism. It requires investigative reporters who can spend months following a single story. It requires data analysts who can parse complex financial records. It requires photographers and camera operators who can capture footage in dangerous places. It requires editors with enough experience to recognize the difference between a promising lead and a wild goose chase. A single comprehensive documentary can run into the millions. These are not expenses that a struggling local paper with three reporters and a photocopier can bear. These are not investments that a foundering digital startup, constantly scrambling for venture capital and ad revenue, can make with any regularity. Only organizations with substantial resources, diversified revenue streams, and the luxury of long-term thinking can afford the kind of journalism that actually matters.

And here is the inconvenient truth that our critics refuse to acknowledge: media consolidation creates exactly those kinds of organizations. When companies merge, when newspapers come under common ownership, when television stations are grouped into networks, something remarkable happens. The efficiencies of scale free up resources that can be redirected toward the work that journalism is supposed to do. The combined entity can share investigative teams across multiple properties. It can afford to keep specialists on payroll who would be luxuries for any single outlet. It can invest in technology and infrastructure that no individual paper could justify. And perhaps most importantly, it can absorb the inevitable losses that come with doing serious journalism—the stories that alienate advertisers, the investigations that provoke retaliation, the accountability work that generates no immediate revenue but serves the public interest nonetheless.

Consider what has happened in the wake of media consolidation. The most celebrated journalistic achievements of our time have come from organizations that could only exist because of scale and resources. The investigative work that exposed corporate corruption, government overreach, and institutional failure has overwhelmingly originated from the newsrooms of major consolidated media companies. These are not accidents. They are the direct result of having the financial strength to pursue stories that matter, even when those stories are expensive, even when they are risky, even when they may never pay for themselves in the short term.

The alternative—the world our critics would have us build—is one where every town has its own paper, every neighborhood has its own broadcaster, and everyone who wants to report the news can do so from their basement with nothing but a laptop and good intentions. This sounds romantic. It sounds like some idealized vision of community journalism, of the fourth estate as a collection of Davids taking on the Goliaths of power. But here is what that world actually looks like: it looks like thousands of outlets that cannot afford to investigate anything, that must churn out whatever content generates the most clicks, that are perpetually one bad month away from shutting down entirely, and that therefore have every incentive to avoid controversy, to copy each other's work, to follow the pack rather than lead it. This is not diversity. This is poverty dressed up as pluralism.

The Natural Working of the Free Market

But my argument extends beyond efficiency. It goes to the very heart of what we believe about economic freedom and the proper role of government in society. The case against media monopolies is, at its core, a case against the free market. It is an argument that the invisible hand, which we trust to allocate resources in every other industry, somehow fails when it comes to the news. It is an assertion that politicians and regulators, who cannot balance their own budgets and cannot run their own agencies efficiently, somehow possess the wisdom to determine what the media landscape should look like.

I reject this premise entirely. I reject it as a matter of philosophy, because I believe that free markets, while imperfect, are vastly superior to central planning in allocating resources to their highest and best uses. And I reject it as a matter of history, because every time governments have attempted to engineer the media landscape—to promote diversity of ownership, to subsidize failing outlets, to impose regulatory burdens on larger companies—the result has been poorer journalism, not richer.

The free market works in media exactly as it works everywhere else. Consumers decide what they want to read, watch, and listen to. Companies that provide what consumers want succeed and grow. Companies that fail to provide value shrink and eventually fail. This process may be messy. It may be painful for those who cannot adapt. But it is the most reliable mechanism we have for matching supply to demand, for rewarding quality, and for weeding out the obsolete and the inefficient.

When we intervene in this process—when we try to preserve failing outlets through subsidies, when we try to prevent mergers through antitrust enforcement, when we try to force diversity of ownership through regulatory mandates—we do not create a healthier media ecosystem. We create a permanently subsidized class of organizations that have no incentive to improve, no mechanism for adjusting to changing consumer preferences, and every incentive to demand ever more protection from the market forces they cannot survive. We create a landscape where the incompetent are preserved at the expense of the excellent, where resources are diverted from winners who could use them to expand and improve, and where consumers are denied the benefits that would come from allowing successful companies to become even more successful.

Consider the empirical evidence. In the decades since the Telecommunications Act of 1996 opened the door to greater media consolidation, what have we actually observed? We have observed the creation of national news organizations with the resources to cover events around the world. We have observed the development of 24-hour news cycles that keep citizens informed in real time. We have observed the rise of digital platforms that can deliver personalized content to billions of people. Are there problems with modern media? Certainly. But those problems—including the decline of local news coverage—are not primarily the result of consolidation. They are the result of technological change, shifts in consumer behavior, and the failure of existing business models to adapt to a digital world. And the solution to those problems is not to turn back the clock to an era of smaller, weaker, poorer news organizations. The solution is to allow the market to continue its work of finding new models that can sustain quality journalism in the digital age.

The Myth of Ownership Diversity

Let me address directly the central myth that animates the anti-monopoly case: the belief that diversity of ownership produces diversity of content. This intuitive-sounding proposition is, upon examination, almost exactly backwards. The evidence suggests that consolidated ownership often produces more varied and distinctive content, while fragmented ownership tends to produce homogeneous content that all looks and sounds the same.

Why? Because larger organizations can afford to take risks. They can afford to experiment with different formats, different voices, different approaches to the news. They can afford to maintain multiple publications with different editorial personalities under the same corporate umbrella. They can invest in specialty coverage that would not be viable for smaller outlets. In other words, scale creates the conditions for diversity within a single organization in a way that fragmented ownership never can.

Meanwhile, the mythical world of maximal ownership diversity—the world of hundreds of competing local papers, each with its own handful of reporters—what does that world actually produce? It produces content farms. It produces wire service stories that are reprinted verbatim across dozens of outlets. It produces a race to the bottom where everyone is covering the same national stories because no one can afford to cover anything else. True diversity of content requires resources. It requires the ability to invest in original reporting, in specialized knowledge, in the kind of journalism that takes time and money to produce. And those resources come from scale.

I would further suggest that the obsession with ownership diversity fundamentally misunderstands what matters in media. What matters is viewpoint diversity, content diversity, the range of ideas and perspectives available to citizens. And there is no reason to believe that having many small owners produces more viewpoint diversity than having fewer large owners. In fact, there are good reasons to believe the opposite. Larger organizations are more likely to have formal editorial processes, fact-checking standards, and institutional cultures that guard against the worst forms of bias. Smaller organizations, answerable to no one and accountable only to their immediate financial pressures, are more likely to fall into partisan lockstep or sensationalism.

The evidence from around the world supports this analysis. Countries with highly fragmented media ownership do not exhibit greater political diversity or healthier democratic debate. If anything, the opposite is true. Fragmented media landscapes tend to be more polarized, more sensational, and more captured by narrow interests than consolidated ones. The reason is simple: small, weak media organizations cannot afford the independence that quality journalism requires. They become dependent on patrons, on advertisers, on political patrons who expect favorable coverage in return. Only strong, well-resourced media organizations have the luxury of telling the truth regardless of whose toes they step on.

The Regulatory Assault on Quality Journalism

I would be remiss if I did not address directly the regulatory apparatus that has been assembled, piece by piece, over the past several decades to constrain media consolidation. This apparatus—encompassing antitrust enforcement, public interest requirements, cross-ownership rules, and a host of other regulations—represents a fundamental misunderstanding of how media markets work and what produces quality journalism.

Consider the effect of antitrust enforcement in media markets. When regulators block mergers, when they require divestitures, when they place conditions on transactions that would otherwise be mutually beneficial, what are they actually doing? They are preventing the creation of organizations that could invest more in journalism, that could achieve efficiencies that would free up resources for reporting, that could compete more effectively in national and international markets. They are preserving a fragmented landscape where no one has the resources to do the kind of job that democracy requires.

And what is the justification for this intervention? The justification is that consolidation reduces competition, and reduced competition supposedly leads to lower quality and higher prices. But this framework, borrowed from the economics of widgets and wheat fields, simply does not apply to media markets. In media, the relationship between competition and quality is not straightforward. Excessive competition—competition for attention in a zero-sum attention economy—can lead to the lowest common denominator, to sensationalism, to the chase for clicks at the expense of substance. The kind of competition that produces quality journalism is competition for reputation, competition for influence, competition to be the source that serious people trust. And that kind of competition is enhanced, not diminished, by consolidation.

Similarly, the public interest obligations that regulators impose on media outlets are, in practice, not requirements to serve the public interest at all. They are requirements to serve the bureaucratic interests of the regulators who impose them, to check boxes and fill out forms, to demonstrate compliance in ways that have nothing to do with whether the journalism actually serves the public. These obligations consume resources that could otherwise go to reporting. They create legal risks that make outlets more cautious about investigating powerful interests. And they establish a framework in which political actors can use the regulatory apparatus to punish media organizations that criticize them.

The proper response to this situation is not to add more regulation, not to impose additional constraints on media ownership, not to create new bureaucracies to oversee the fourth estate. The proper response is to recognize that the market, imperfect as it is, does a better job of allocating resources to journalism than any planning mechanism could. It is to trust consumers to decide what they want to read and watch. It is to allow media organizations to fail when they do not provide value and to succeed when they do. And it is to focus government intervention not on the structure of media ownership but on ensuring that the basic rules of the game—property rights, contract enforcement, protection against libel and slander—are applied consistently and fairly to all participants in the market.

A Vision for the Future

I want to conclude by offering a vision of what a truly free media market could look like—a market unburdened by the anti-competitive restrictions that currently constrain it, free to consolidate where consolidation creates value, free to experiment with new models, free to invest in journalism that matters.

In this vision, we would see the emergence of even more powerful media organizations—organizations with the resources to cover every corner of the globe, to maintain bureaus in every capital city, to investigate every significant abuse of power regardless of how many millions it costs. We would see competition not among dozens of impoverished outlets fighting over scraps, but among a handful of well-resourced organizations competing on the quality of their journalism, the depth of their analysis, and the reliability of their reporting. We would see innovation in business models, as these organizations experiment with different ways of sustaining quality journalism in the digital age—subscriptions, memberships, philanthropy, events, and hybrid approaches we have not yet imagined.

And we would see, I believe, a renaissance in journalism itself. Because when you give reporters and editors the resources they need, when you free them from the constant anxiety of whether the next month's payroll will clear, when you assure them that their organizations can survive the inevitable controversies that come with doing real journalism—you create the conditions for work that can genuinely inform the public, hold power accountable, and strengthen democracy.

This is not a vision of media uniformity or homogenization. It is a vision of media excellence—a landscape in which the highest quality journalism is rewarded with the resources to do even better, in which mediocrity is allowed to fade away, and in which citizens have access to information and analysis of a caliber that our current fragmented, impoverished system cannot provide.

Conclusion

Ladies and gentlemen, the case for media monopolies is not a case against competition. It is a case for competition on the terms that actually matter—competition to produce the best journalism, to serve the most readers, to build the most trusted brands. It is a case for trusting the market rather than the regulators, for allowing scale where scale creates value, for recognizing that quality journalism requires resources and that resources require success.

The enemies of media consolidation would have you believe that they are defending democracy against concentrations of power. But the truth is exactly the opposite. By preventing the creation of strong, well-resourced media organizations, they are ensuring that no one has the power to investigate the powerful, that no one has the resources to tell the stories that need to be told, and that journalism remains permanently impoverished, permanently dependent, permanently afraid.

I say: let us build a media system that has the power to hold anyone accountable. I say: let us trust the free market to determine the optimal structure of media ownership. I say: let us stop listening to the myths and start looking at the evidence, which shows that consolidation produces better journalism, more efficient markets, and a stronger democracy.

Thank you.

In Defense of Big Media: Why Consolidation Serves Journalism, Consumers, and Democracy

Since 2005, more than 2,500 American newspapers have closed. News deserts spread across the country, statehouse press corps have hollowed out, and entire communities now go without a single full-time reporter. This catastrophe unfolded under a regime of strict ownership restrictions, cross-ownership bans, and regulatory suspicion of media mergers—rules that were supposed to protect the very ecosystem now collapsing. The lesson should be obvious: the conventional wisdom has it backward. Consolidation did not kill local journalism; the digital advertising revolution did. Consolidation is the industry's attempt to survive that revolution—and blocking it only hastens the funeral. Concentrated media ownership, far from menacing the public interest, offers the best remaining hope of funding it. Scale delivers the capital that quality journalism requires, the efficiency that modern markets demand, and the innovation that audiences expect. Policymakers should stop fighting consolidation and start welcoming it.

The Economics of Journalism Demand Scale

Journalism has an unusual cost structure: enormous fixed costs and near-zero marginal costs. Reporting, editing, fact-checking, and legal review are expensive; delivering the finished product to one additional reader costs essentially nothing. Industries with this structure naturally gravitate toward large firms, because average costs fall as output grows. This is not a defect to be corrected—it is economics to be harnessed. A regional media group can spread the cost of an investigative unit, a data journalism team, or a printing plant across dozens of outlets. A standalone owner cannot.

Indeed, economists have long recognized that local news approximates a natural monopoly: by the late twentieth century, the vast majority of American cities supported exactly one daily newspaper, not because regulators allowed it, but because the market would bear only one. Ownership rules cannot legislate competition into a market whose economics forbid it. They can only guarantee that the single surviving outlet is undercapitalized rather than well-funded. The real choice in most communities is not between many owners and one. It is between one strong owner and none.

Large organizations also perform a function that fragmented ones cannot: cross-subsidy. Joseph Schumpeter observed that firms with market power are often the engines of progress precisely because their scale lets them fund ventures with uncertain returns. Media history bears this out. Profitable divisions of major companies have long carried prestige journalism that could never pay its own way—foreign bureaus, investigative teams, documentary units. Strip away scale, and you strip away the surplus that makes public-interest journalism possible.

Quality Follows Capital

Serious journalism is staggeringly expensive. A major investigation can consume months of reporter time, thousands in document litigation, and six figures in legal review before a single word is published. This is why the landmark accountability journalism of recent decades has come overwhelmingly from large, well-capitalized organizations. When the Boston Globe's Spotlight team exposed the Catholic Church abuse scandal—investigative work so consequential it became an Oscar-winning film—the Globe was owned by the New York Times Company, a national corporation whose resources sustained a local investigative unit no standalone paper could have afforded. When Jeff Bezos purchased the Washington Post in 2013, the paper was widely written off as a dying institution. Deep-pocketed ownership invested hundreds of millions in technology and talent, expanded the newsroom, multiplied its digital audience, and returned it to profitability. That is what concentrated ownership buys.

Contrast this with the romantic fiction that small, independent ownership guarantees editorial virtue. The independent local press of the nineteenth century was fiercely partisan, often functioning as an open organ of political machines. Atomized ownership produced sensationalism and party propaganda, not golden-age objectivity. Editorial quality has always followed institutional strength—the resources to hire the best journalists, defend them in court, and publish what powerful interests want suppressed.

Efficiency Is Not a Dirty Word

Merger critics fixate on post-consolidation layoffs, but this mistakes the undertaker for the disease. Newsroom jobs disappeared because classified advertising migrated to Craigslist and local advertising migrated to Google and Meta—trends that would have devastated small owners faster than large ones. A merged newsroom of forty journalists is not a tragedy compared to the alternative: two bankrupt newsrooms of zero.

The efficiency gains from consolidation are real and substantial. Combined printing, distribution, advertising sales, technology infrastructure, and administrative functions free capital for the one thing that matters: reporting. Nor is duplication a virtue. Two struggling outlets each sending a stenographer to the same school board meeting, while neither can afford a single data journalist, is not diversity—it is waste dressed up as pluralism. Consolidation converts redundancy into depth.

Antitrust law, properly understood, exists to protect consumers, not to preserve a particular industrial structure or shelter competitors from competition. Under the consumer welfare standard associated with Robert Bork, the question is whether a merger raises prices or degrades products. In media, the evidence runs the other way: consolidated companies offer bundled content, better apps, wider distribution, and free ad-supported journalism. Where consolidation demonstrably harms consumers, existing antitrust law already provides the remedy. Reflexive structural prohibitions—rules against owning too much, regardless of effect—are relics of an era when regulators confused bigness with badness.

Innovation Requires Scale—and the Real Giants Are Elsewhere

Digital transformation is brutally capital-intensive. Podcast studios, video operations, recommendation engines, mobile apps, AI-assisted reporting tools: each demands investment that only large organizations can fund and the patience to absorb failures along the way. The New York Times's transformation into a digital powerhouse—eleven million subscribers, a portfolio spanning news, games, cooking, and audio—required years of sustained investment that a fragmented industry could never have mounted. Its acquisition of The Athletic gave a promising but cash-burning startup a permanent home, rescuing hundreds of sports journalism jobs through consolidation.

Meanwhile, the "monopoly" framing collapses under scrutiny of the actual market. Media companies compete in an attention economy dominated by Google, Meta, Amazon, and TikTok—platforms that capture the lion's share of digital advertising revenue and face no comparable ownership constraints. Measured in that relevant market, even the largest newspaper chains are minnows. It is perverse to shackle domestic media companies with structural ownership caps while the platforms that destroyed their business model operate at planetary scale. Permitting consolidation is the minimum condition for traditional journalism to compete with Big Tech at all.

Diversity Is Safer Than Ever

Ownership limits were born of scarcity: the Supreme Court's Red Lion decision justified broadcast regulation on the ground that the electromagnetic spectrum was finite. The internet abolished that scarcity. Today anyone with a phone can publish to a global audience; Substack writers, YouTube journalists, nonprofit newsrooms, and podcasters have created a long tail of voices more diverse than anything the three-network era produced. The viewpoint diversity that ownership rules were designed to protect now flourishes entirely outside the regulated sphere. Concentration among legacy owners simply does not translate into concentration of available perspectives.

Nor does consolidation extinguish pluralism within organizations. Large media companies maintain distinct brands, editorial boards, and newsroom cultures across their properties—and they are disciplined by the market to do so, because a news brand's entire commercial value rests on its credibility. An owner who corrupts a trusted product destroys the asset they purchased. The market polices editorial integrity more effectively than any FCC rulebook ever has.

Regulation Has Failed—Why Extend It?

The regulatory track record is one of unambiguous failure. The FCC's newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership ban, imposed in 1975, persisted into the smartphone era and survived nearly two decades of litigation before its repeal. While regulators spent years on quadrennial reviews, technology transformed the industry in months. The rules did not save local news—the closures happened anyway, on the regulators' watch. Worse, ownership restrictions froze capital out of the industry precisely when investment was most desperately needed, and when strategic buyers were chilled, distressed assets fell to financial buyers with no interest in journalism whatsoever.

There is also a deeper principle at stake. A government empowered to decide who may own news organizations holds a weapon that can be turned against the press itself. The First Amendment's logic cuts toward keeping the state at arm's length from decisions about media ownership, not toward giving regulators a veto over it.

Conclusion

The debate over media consolidation is haunted by nostalgia for a world of three networks and two-daily towns—a world the internet has permanently destroyed. The genuine threat to journalism today is not too much capital but too little. Scale funds the investigations, builds the technology, sustains the cross-subsidies, and provides the competitive mass to stand up to the platforms. The alternative to consolidation is not competition; it is closure. Policymakers should repeal the anachronistic ownership rules, evaluate mergers on evidence of actual consumer harm rather than reflexive suspicion of size, and let media companies become big enough to do journalism well.

Allowing large-scale media consolidation—up to and including the formation of dominant firms or even “monopolies” in particular local or niche markets—is not an ideological preference but a pragmatic conclusion about how high-quality journalism is produced, how markets allocate scarce resources, and how innovation is sustained in industries defined by enormous fixed costs. Consolidated ownership can improve editorial capacity, generate efficiencies that make long-term reporting feasible, and spur technological and organizational innovation. In that context, the case for extensive regulatory intervention is weaker than critics claim: regulation often substitutes political judgment for market discipline, raising costs without reliably improving the public’s access to better information.

1) Consolidation can raise the quality of journalism by funding the costly parts of reporting

The most important work in modern journalism—investigations, document-heavy reporting, international correspondence, litigation-risk coverage, data journalism, and sustained beat reporting—is expensive and time-consuming. These activities share two features: they require significant upfront investment, and they do not necessarily “pay back” immediately through short-term audience metrics.

When media outlets are fragmented across many small owners, they often face a chronic funding problem. Smaller firms must prioritize content that is cheap, fast, and reliably viral because their revenue base is narrow and their tolerance for unprofitable undertakings is limited. In contrast, larger consolidated companies can spread fixed costs across multiple properties, pay for specialized editorial talent, and underwrite projects that will only earn returns later—or not at all, but still serve the public interest.

In this sense, consolidation can function like a professionalization engine. Scale makes it possible to support newsroom roles that smaller entities cannot sustain: editors with legal expertise, technologists for verification and data analysis, researchers for source development, and producers who can manage complex multimedia investigations. If the goal is better journalism, the structure that reliably finances journalism’s most expensive components is an economic question—not simply a moral one.

2) Concentrated ownership promotes market efficiency by reducing duplication and reallocating resources

Critics often treat consolidation as inherently harmful, assuming that reducing the number of owners must reduce the variety of views. But market efficiency is about resource allocation, not headcount. Media markets include large sunk costs in infrastructure: reporting operations, distribution relationships, ad and subscription systems, content management, and compliance.

Without scale, many firms duplicate identical functions. Multiple small companies simultaneously create costly editorial teams, bargain separately for advertising and carriage, maintain separate technology stacks, and rebuild similar workflows. Consolidation eliminates redundant overhead and reallocates those resources toward core content production and experimentation. This is not merely cost-cutting; it is the removal of waste that otherwise depresses the ability of outlets to invest in quality.

In an efficient market, firms that become large are often doing so because they can serve audiences and advertisers better—through packaging, reliability, speed, geographic reach, or credibility. When a consolidated company can lower average costs per story and improve distribution effectiveness, it can afford to offer more consistent coverage and fewer “gaps” in reporting. That kind of operational stability is a prerequisite for sustained editorial excellence.

3) Dominant firms can create stronger incentives for innovation

Innovation in media is capital-intensive and risk-laden. Whether the innovation is a new subscription product, a verification platform, an audio/video format, AI-assisted newsroom tooling (with appropriate safeguards), or a restructuring of how content is delivered across devices, it requires funding and organizational capacity.

Consolidated ownership can provide exactly that. When firms earn sufficient scale-backed revenues, they can finance experimentation without immediately sacrificing long-term capability. Importantly, innovation is not only about new technology; it is also about process innovation—how editorial standards are maintained, how sources are verified, how content is personalized responsibly, and how platforms respond to changing consumption habits.

By contrast, under fragmented ownership, firms may “innovate” in ways that are superficial and short-cycle because they cannot afford long development timelines. Consolidation can therefore shift incentives from cheap, incremental changes toward deeper investments that improve both the product and the underlying editorial workflow.

4) “Competition” does not require many owners; it requires pressure and alternatives

A common objection is that monopolies reduce competition and thereby reduce quality or diversity. But competition in media does not depend solely on the number of ownership entities. It depends on whether audiences and advertisers have meaningful alternatives that discipline pricing, responsiveness, and performance.

Even in consolidated markets, outlets often compete across platforms—print, broadcast, digital, streaming, podcasts, newsletters, and independent online creators. Consumers can switch between providers quickly, advertisers can reallocate budgets across channels, and new entrants can target underserved audiences. Consolidation may reduce ownership count, but it does not necessarily eliminate competitive pressure.

Moreover, viewers and readers are not passive. The market rewards credibility and responsiveness. If a dominant firm mishandles quality—through sensationalism, systematic inaccuracy, or editorial neglect—audiences can and do migrate to substitutes. That consumer-driven discipline is a real, ongoing check on editorial sloppiness.

5) Regulatory intervention is often a blunt tool that undermines dynamism and raises costs

If consolidation tends to improve quality through scale, efficiency, and investment capacity, then the burden of proof shifts to regulation. Yet many regulatory proposals are designed as if the main problem is corporate concentration itself, not the economic incentives concentration can create.

Regulatory intervention—especially structural rules aimed at preventing large mergers or imposing complex ownership limits—can slow the very process by which struggling news organizations stabilize their finances and modernize their operations. It can also shift firms’ behavior away from long-term investment toward legal compliance and litigation risk management. That is an economic distortion: scarce capital goes into avoiding restrictions rather than improving reporting and building new capabilities.

In addition, regulators face a knowledge problem. They are asked to evaluate editorial outcomes, market dynamics, and future innovation trajectories with incomplete information. The result is often inconsistent policy, delayed decision-making, and uncertainty that discourages investment at the exact moment media firms need scale to adapt.

Better journalism, on this view, is not achieved by bureaucratic micromanagement of ownership structures; it is achieved through incentives that fund the hard work of reporting. If consolidation funds that work more effectively than fragmentation, regulation risks doing the opposite of what it intends.

Conclusion

Large-scale media consolidation can be defended—not as an abstract economic ideal, but as a practical mechanism for producing better journalism, improving market efficiency, and enabling innovation. By pooling resources, reducing duplicated overhead, supporting expensive reporting, and financing long-term experimentation, consolidated firms can deliver a more robust editorial product than a landscape of small, undercapitalized competitors. While concerns about diversity and power deserve serious discussion, heavy-handed regulatory intervention is not the right remedy. The more coherent approach is to recognize the economic logic of why media industries consolidate—and to allow market forces to determine which ownership structures best sustain high-quality information in a demanding and rapidly changing environment.
